one_line: Jordi Spranger (Spranic, with Neo4j) pitches walk-through 3D scans stored as a time-aligned graph, so real buildings become queryable, change-tracked data for insurance and lending.
summary: The speaker argues that real estate, the largest asset class at about 400 trillion globally, is tracked in financial books updated quarterly while the buildings themselves are only re-checked every few years. He proposes "spatial memory": anyone walks a space with an off-the-shelf sensor, a scan is produced in about a minute, and recognised objects are stored in a Neo4j graph. Repeat walks are aligned on a time axis so that object-by-object changes can be detected, and each observation keeps a reference to its source capture as evidence. The map can then be queried in natural language, with examples such as finding a radiator or a mug in a kitchen, and displaced chairs shown as a change between two passes. The main use case is insurance, where a renewal walk gives the insurer a delta to price against, with cited figures on underinsurance and certification discounts. The talk is a short product pitch from a company founded in June 2026, so the claims are largely unverified in the talk itself.

key_ideas.detail: Financial books on buildings are updated quarterly, but the physical assets behind them are only re-checked about every few years, leaving a black box between updates.

key_ideas.idea: Capture a building by walking it
key_ideas.detail: An off-the-shelf sensor is walked through a space; the speaker says a scan is ready about a minute later, and recognised assets are written into a graph database.

key_ideas.idea: Repeat walks align on a time axis
key_ideas.detail: Each walk is kept as a time-stamped layer, so the same space can be compared across months or quarters and its evolution tracked.

key_ideas.idea: Ask ledger-style questions of a building
key_ideas.detail: The required questions are what changed, when it changed (each observation carries its source), and who must be told about the delta.
In a kitchen demo, three displaced chairs are flagged between two passes, and the answer links back to the capture that shows the change.
An initial walk at policy start and a second walk at renewal give the insurer a measured upkeep delta to price premiums against.

techniques.name: Repeat-capture alignment and diffing
techniques.how: Capture the same space at several points in time, match objects between captures, and compare them object by object and surrounding by surrounding to get a delta.
techniques.when: Any domain where the same environment is snapshotted repeatedly and you need to know what changed.

techniques.name: Graph as the world model
techniques.how: Store recognised objects and spaces as graph nodes and link each observation to its capture, so new relationships and attributes can be added per asset.
techniques.when: When the data needs flexible, asset-specific connections rather than a fixed schema.

techniques.name: Provenance on every observation
techniques.how: Attach a reference to the originating capture to each fact so claims can be checked against the raw evidence.
techniques.when: Audit, insurance or compliance settings where a claim must be backed by source material.

techniques.name: Natural-language query over a graph map
techniques.how: Let users ask questions of the mapped space and return answers tied to specific objects, with the delta and source shown.
techniques.when: When non-technical users need to query structured spatial data.

numbers.claim: Real estate is about 400 trillion globally, more than global equities, debt and gold combined (residential ~300T, commercial ~60T, agriculture ~50T)
Kroll research on 1,500 properties found about 70% of buildings underinsured (speaker does not know the cause)
The underinsurance problem affects about 4 trillion US commercial mortgages
Real estate records are typically updated about every 5 years (year 0 to year 5 gap)
A full scan of a conference hall took about a minute of walking
One in three commercial buildings are on the books with the wrong construction class
A 35% hurricane-premium deduction is available for certified buildings
73% of insurers agree they claim fewer hurricane damages when buildings are checked and certified (transcript reads '70% 73%', exact figure unclear)

hot_takes: A building should be as queryable as a ledger, answering in milliseconds rather than after a site visit.
Every walk should become a memory of the building.
Insurance should be priced on measured, verified property upkeep rather than old, coarse records.

relevance.why: MemoryMesh could use the same idea of time-aligned, provenance-linked observations across sessions, but the talk gives no retrieval or consistency detail.
relevance.action: Read the talk's time-aligned provenance pattern as a loose idea for MemoryMesh conflict resolution and provenance; no implementation change needed yet.

relevance.why: No relevance to Claude Code harnessing, checkpoints or approvals.
Matching the same object across two captures is an entity-alignment problem, which is a recurring interest, but the talk does not describe the method.
relevance.action: Skip unless a real-world-asset or spatial-data project comes up; the talk has no transferable technique detail.
